briefs: docs/round10/track-m2.md (read M20 and docs/round10/track-d0.md D0-2 and D0-3 first)
notes: Round 10 runs several tracks at once, each in its own worktree: D0 (shared mob registry), D (trial spawners, vaults, lodestones, breezes), W (darkness, vibrations, sculk, warden), E1 and E2 (known limits), F (Elden Ring boss) and the mob tracks M1 (land animals), M2 (this run: water mobs and buckets) and M3 (night, built mobs and horses), which all plug into D0's registry. Never bump minecraft_net::PROTOCOL, even where a brief says to: the release step bumps it once when messages changed; if a commit changes a ToClient/ToServer message or the codec, add a line under '## Protocol' in the track log. Insert new enum variants, match arms and list entries next to related ones, not at the end of lists, to keep merges small. Record decisions in the track log. M2 edits only its own water group files (entities world/families/water*, world natural_spawner/families/water.rs, terrain families/water*) and the M2 section of docs/round10/mobs.md, plus the shared lines its brief names; every shared piece has one owner in the brief's M20 tables, so never build a copy of an M1, M3, E or W piece: if a group's M20 wait is not met in this branch, leave that group, note it in the log, and go on with the groups that do not need it. RESTARTS: if this run was started again after a stop (the PC crashed on 2026-10-28 at 20:27 with six tracks building), the worktree may hold the current group's half-done work as uncommitted or staged changes: read `git status` and `git diff` (and `git diff --cached`) first, keep what is correct, finish the group and commit it; discard only what is broken. If cargo reports invalid or corrupt metadata, a truncated .rlib/.rmeta or a link error on a file that should exist, run `& .\scripts\cargo-slot.ps1 +target=<this track's target> clean -p <crate>` for that crate and build again. LOAD: builds now run at -j 4 per slot to keep the laptop cool; never start a second cargo command, the game, or any other long CPU-heavy process.
